# Does Your Law Firm’s Website Answer the Questions Clients Actually Ask?


By OpenTools Team


Listen to ten new‑client calls, and a pattern usually appears. People ask about cost, timing, what happens next, whether they have a case, what documents they need, and how a legal problem can affect work or family. Then visit many law firm websites, and those questions are hard to find.


Effective[SEO for law firm](https://hennessey.com/law-firm-seo/) websites starts with the language real clients use. Search data can show what people type into Google, while intake calls, emails, chat logs, and consultation notes reveal what they ask after they find the firm. Those two sources can guide content that attracts attention and helps someone decide what to do next.


## **Use Intake as Research**


The intake team hears questions that keyword tools cannot fully explain.


A personal injury caller can ask whether using health insurance will hurt a claim. A divorce client can ask who stays in the house while the case is pending. A criminal defense caller can ask whether an employer will find out about an arrest.


Write these questions down. Group them by practice area and note which ones appear repeatedly.


This creates a content list based on real concerns instead of guesses made during a marketing meeting.


## **Answer the Question Before Selling**


A visitor who asks, “How long do I have to file?” wants an answer before reading why the firm is different.


Give the useful explanation first. State the general rule, then explain the facts that can change it. If an exception matters, describe it in plain language.


After helping the reader understand the issue, the page can explain why legal advice becomes important.


This order builds trust because the content earns attention instead of demanding it.


## **Match One Page to One Need**


One giant page cannot answer every question well.


A practice area page needs to explain the service and the main legal process. Separate articles can go deeper into narrower questions. An FAQ section can handle short questions that need brief answers.


The format needs to fit the subject.


A question about what to bring to a consultation can be answered in a short checklist. A question about how fault is decided in a truck crash needs more explanation. A question about whether a conviction can be cleared requires details about eligibility and limits.


Do not force every topic into the same template.


## **Write the Way Clients Speak**


Potential clients rarely search with the exact language used in statutes.


They ask, “Can I move with my child after divorce?” rather than naming a relocation statute. They ask, “Who pays my medical bills after a crash?” rather than searching for a technical damages term.


Use the client’s wording in headings and introductions, then explain the legal term when it becomes useful.


This does not mean avoiding legal accuracy. It means translating the law into language that a person can understand before hiring a lawyer.


## **Cover the Next Question Too**


A strong answer creates another question.


If a page explains that a person has a filing deadline, the reader also needs to know when the clock starts, what can change the deadline, and what happens if evidence is still being collected.


If a page explains bail, the reader may also need information about release conditions, future hearings, and what happens if a condition is broken.


Think through the sequence from the client’s point of view.[Useful content](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/tips-creating-amazing-content/294435/) follows the problem forward instead of stopping after one definition.


## **Check Whether the Content Works**


Traffic alone cannot tell you whether a page answers the right question.


Look at calls, forms, chat conversations, and the pages people visit before contacting the firm. Ask intake staff whether callers still seem confused about issues the website claims to explain.


Old pages also need review. Laws change, court procedures change, attorneys leave firms, and service areas expand. A page that answered the question correctly three years ago can become misleading today.


Google’s people‑first content guidance also rewards a basic idea that fits legal marketing well: create information because it helps the reader, not because a keyword exists.


A law firm website becomes more useful when it sounds like a good first conversation with the firm. It answers the question clearly, explains what changes the answer, and gives the reader a sensible next step. That is the kind of content people can use before they ever pick up the phone.
